body_markdown:
Shahin Armin grew up in Iran. The Paykan, that country’s national car, which was produced for 38 years starting in 1967, was a touchstone of his entire life there. When he was born, it had been on sale for almost a decade, and by the time he and his sister emigrated to the United States just before the turn of the 21st century, millions of the little sedans and its pickup truck cousins filled their homeland’s roads.


Actually, it would be a misrepresentation to say the Paykan was just part of Armin’s former life in Iran, as he may currently be the world’s biggest Paykan enthusiast. A car guy in general, though, he’s not just an enthusiast of Paykans. His daily driver is a 2008 Acura TL, and he has a 2001 BMW 540i and a Suzuki DR650 motorcycle for fun. He keeps a 1973 BMW 2002 in Tehran, but the Paykan—Persian for “arrow”—was his first automotive love and he has owned four of them.


Iran National


Armin’s affection for the Paykan is clear from watching *Iran’s Arrow* : *The Rise and Fall of Paykan* , a 78-minute documentary he and co-director Sohrab Daryabandari created about the car, its history, and its role in Iran’s culture. A labor of love, the award-winning Persian language film took almost five years to complete. The result dramatically illustrates that no matter what differences people around the world may have, car enthusiasts are pretty much the same.


Armin, 49, currently works for Ford as an automotive design engineer and has a CV that includes stints at Chrysler and Honda. He says that you can tell a lot about a society and a country by its car culture, and if ever a car was intertwined with a culture, it would be the Paykan and Iran. The Paykan survived literal revolutionary changes in Iran as it became deeply rooted in that society, extending its influence beyond mere transportation to music and art. So deeply rooted that *Tavalodet Mobarak* , a jingle from a 1969 commercial celebrating the Paykan’s third birthday, is now the song Iranians sing for their own birthdays.


Iran’s beloved singer, Hayede, the country’s counterpart to Egypt’s Umm Kulthum, or maybe America’s Dolly Parton, even recorded a version with the song’s composer, Anoushiravan Rohani.


Painting by Hossein Soltani


Long before Uber and Lyft existed, a generation of Iranians survived the privations of the Iran-Iraq War (1980–88) by putting their Paykans into service as *mosāferkesh* , gypsy cabs, and there was a time that orange Paykan taxis were as common on Tehran streets as yellow Checkers once were in Manhattan.


Paykan taxi.


Courtesy Iran's Arrow


Today, few Paykans are still on the road, mostly in Iran’s smaller, poorer cities, but there is a growing community of young Paykan enthusiasts who are as eager about their cars as you would find at any cars and coffee or concours d’elegance. In 2023, more than[600 Paykan owners, most of them born long after the car was introduced, displayed their cars and trucks](https://en.mehrnews.com/photo/200317/Paykan-exhibition-at-Milad-Tower) at a show in Tehran to celebrate the Paykan’s 56th birthday.


Shahin Armin


What is a national car? It’s an automobile intended to put a country on the road to modernity by domestically producing it for that nation’s as yet unmotored masses, not only to provide personal transportation but also to spur industrial development. As Egyptian dictator Gamal Abdel Nasser said, “A country that can produce cars can produce anything.” Examples of national cars have been Nazi Germany’s Volkswagen Beetle, East Germany’s Trabant, Russia’s Lada, Israel’s Sussita, and India’s Hindustan Ambassador.


One of the most successful national cars, in terms of production and sales, and perhaps the one that has had the greatest cultural impact on its own nation, has been Iran’s Paykan, with about 3 million sedans produced from 1967 to 2005. To that number add thousands and thousands of the locally engineered Paykan “Vanet” pickup truck, still in common use by tradesmen, small businesses, and farmers, which was in production even longer, from 1969 until 2015. Between the sedan, wagon, and pickup, at 48 years, that puts the Paykan as one of the longest produced platforms in automotive history, along with the likes of the[Fiat 124](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1973-fiat-124-special-sedan/) and BMC Mini.


A lot has changed in Iran since the Paykan was introduced. Here a Paykan graces the May/June 1973 cover of popular weekly women’s magazine *Zan-e Rooz* with Sousan Hakima, who competed as Miss Iran in the International Teen Princess competition.


Kayhan Publishing Company


The Paykan was a somewhat localized version of the Rootes Group’s mid-size (U.K. scale) sedan introduced in 1966, which was sold under a variety of brands and model names marketed by the organizationally chaotic manufacturer. Best known as the Hillman Hunter, the car was also sold, among other nameplates, as the Singer Gazelle, the Humber Sceptre, and the Sunbeam Rapier. Depending on the trim level and body style, as well as U.K. or export markets, there were at least 40 different badge-engineered versions. In some French-speaking markets the wagon was elegantly called the Hillman Break de Chasse (Shooting Break). After Chrysler completed its acquisition of the Rootes Group in early 1967, the platform was even sold in the United States as the Sunbeam Arrow, with ads somewhat surprisingly calling it “posh” with “baby-limousine comforts.”


Chrysler


Though for years Armin has searched for the reason why Iran National, the company that introduced the Paykan, picked Rootes and specifically the Arrow for licensing, he’s never found a clear answer. The company was founded in 1962 as the Iran National Industrial Manufacturing Company by brothers Ahmad and Mahmoud Khayami.


Paykan pickups used to sell produce.


Courtesy Iran's Arrow


He does know that the Khayamis signed a contract with Rootes in 1964, two years before Arrow production began in the U.K., that the two companies worked closely on the Iranian launch, and that Rootes placed considerable trust in the Iranian firm, which started assembly only six months after U.K. builds began. It should be pointed out that many national car startups have typically involved local licensed assembly of “completely knocked down” (CKD) kits, and some sources say that is how the first Paykans were made. However, according to Armin, from day one of production, bodies were assembled from panels supplied by a stamping plant on the outskirts of Tehran. Eventually, all of the Paykan was locally produced. Various Rootes brands’ trim parts and things like bumpers were picked off the parts shelf to give the Paykan a unique look.


Wikimedia Commons/Nevit Dilmen


In all likelihood, Rootes was chosen because, like many independent automakers in the 1960s, it was desperate for business. Company managers possibly preferred to license their little Mini competitor,[the technically interesting Imp](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/this-little-imp-helped-kill-off-the-big-rootes-group/) , powered by a detuned Coventry Climax racing engine, as it was faring badly against the groundbreaking front-wheel driver from Austin. However, the Imp was a subcompact, and the five-passenger Arrow made more sense as a family car.


Paykan assembly begins, 1967.


Courtesy Iran National


American automakers didn’t need the business and may have preferred setting up a subsidiary or a joint venture as General Motors did for assembling Opels, Chevrolets, and Cadillacs. Larger European companies like Fiat did not want their exports to compete with locally produced licensed assembly. Iran National probably went with Rootes for the same reasons Israel’s Autocar got a license from Reliant to make the Sussita; Rootes was a willing and eager partner.


Khosro Dahaghin’s shop in Roudehen, outside of Tehran, restores Iran-built Cadillac Sevilles.


Instagram


Rather than being posh and limousine like, in fact the Arrow was basic transportation. It was a conventional four-door sedan with a front-mounted inline 1.8-liter four-cylinder engine driving the rear wheels through a four-speed manual transmission, and suspended with McPherson struts up front and leaf springs in the back. Being basic, though, meant the Persian version was fairly reliable, easy to service, and durable. As much as the one Paykan hater featured in *Iran’s Arrow* loathes the car’s primitive nature, a factory-supported Hillman Hunter indeed won the rigorous[1968 London to Sydney Marathon](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6_kEPhEMSFY) , beating many far more prestigious brands. The rally’s route actually took the Paykan sibling directly through Iran, though it’s unclear how much local publicity the race generated, as to this day most Iranians know nothing about it.


The 1968 London to Sydney Marathon winner.


Flickr/IainCameron


It’s not that there weren’t cars made in Iran before the Paykan. The last Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, was a notable automobile enthusiast who encouraged the development of a domestic auto industry. By the late 1970s, when he was deposed in the Islamic Revolution, you could get locally assembled cars, from the Citroën Dyane to[Cadillac Sevilles](https://mashinname.ir/american-cars-history-iran/) . Armin explained that at the time, Tehran was the only place outside of the United States where Cadillacs were assembled.


The shah inspects a Paykan at the factory’s inauguration.


Bamshad Magazine/Public Domain


As mentioned, Armin is an engineer. He didn’t go to film school, but he and his co-director shot and edited the film themselves. And they did, as mentioned, an award-winning job. *Iran’s Arrow* had its origins in 2009, when Armin started publishing PaykanHunter.com. Three years later, in 2012, he wanted to take a year off for an extended trip back to Iran and explore his roots. With a dream of making a documentary about the Paykan, he first co-curated two fine art exhibitions of Paykan related works from some of the country’s most prominent artists. Armin says that he felt it was his civic duty to make the film and decided to then stay in Iran and turn that dream into reality.


The last Paykan produced, on display in 2005.


AFP via Getty Images


Armin’s love for movies began as a small child. After the revolution, it was not easy to get Hollywood movies in Iran, so bootlegs on VHS circulated. His father, an architect, was a film lover, with a passion for science fiction and the work of director Stanley Kubrick, and they would watch those films together. Around the time Armin immigrated to the United States, successful documentaries from filmmakers like Ken Burns and Michael Moore alerted him to the possibilities of that genre.


Filmmakers Shahin Armin (left) and Sohrab Daryabandari


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


Once he decided to have the film made, which he said came at considerable financial and personal cost, he found his co-director in Sohrab Daryabandari and the two started planning, shooting, and editing the documentary—a process that took more than two years. Getting permits and clearances just be able to film in public on location in Iran would sometimes take months. Despite the difficulties and delays, the two men prevailed and the film premiered in 2017 in Tehran to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the Paykan. It ran in the capital for four months, to some acclaim, followed by a successful tour of showings around Iran. Since then, Armin has been doing screenings at documentary festivals around the world and at special showings, such as at the Detroit Film Theater, where I saw it recently. I videotaped the question-and-answer session with Armin after the screening.


One striking impression from the film was how primitive automobile assembly was 60 years ago, when production of the Paykan began, with workers torch welding parts of the unibody and spacing structural spot welds by hand, with minimal protective equipment. Archive photos show the same processes were still in place past the 1990s, when much of the world’s automotive industry had already switched to robotic welding for better quality control and employee safety.


An Paykan assembly line worker does it the old fashioned way…


Shepard Sherbell/Getty


Perhaps my favorite part of *Iran’s Arrow* is a sequence of scenes that by themselves would make an elegant and moving short film if they were stitched together but instead are interspersed throughout the movie. At the start of the film we see an older man taking his Paykan out for a drive. He takes a soft cloth and lovingly, almost reverently, dusts off the entire car, polishing the chrome trim in the process. He gets behind the wheel, inserts and twists the ignition key, releases the parking brake and drives off. He pops up here and there later in the film, driving the car in an urban setting. The driver is never identified and he never says a word in any of the scenes in which he appears. Just an Iranian everyman with his Paykan. Finally, we see him parking the Paykan, locking it, and walking away into an alley.


*Iran’s Arrow* is an engaging documentary about a dearly beloved national car, filmed against a background subject that can get very complicated. Some sensitive subject matters may not be addressed directly in the film, but the choices and juxtaposition of images and scenes can sometimes make a stronger impression than explicit exposition.


In case you’re intrigued and want to own a Paykan, according to Armin there are no real Paykans in North America and possibly just 40 U.K. variants. As far as he knows, no U.S. market Sunbeam Arrows still exist. The government of Iran prohibited the export of cars after some of the cars in the shah’s collection were smuggled out of the country. Armin says to beware of counterfeit Paykans that are actually RHD Rootes-brand cars imported from the U.K., which have been converted to left-hand drive and “Paykanized” with parts from Rootes variants. The dead giveaway on those cars, he says, is the configuration of the windshield wipers, which won’t properly clear the glass in front of the driver. He can also check off other red flags, just like a vintage Gibson Les Paul collector spotting the inaccuracies of a counterfeit, Chinese-made “Chibson” guitar. Armin himself imported a Singer Gazelle variant from the U.K. but no longer owns it, and yes, he does regret selling it. If he could import a Paykan, it would be the rare, sporty Javanan (Youth) model, which had cast wheels, better instrumentation, and more supportive seats, but also an aluminum cylinder head, dual carbs, and about 94 horsepower, compared to a regular Paykan’s roughly 70 hp.


Paykan Javanan


[Ronnie Schreiber](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/rschreiber/)


[There will be a showing of Iran’s Arrow on Friday, November 13, at the Moto cafe in Ferndale, just north of Detroit.](https://motomichigan.com/eventsandrentals/p/iransarrowdocumentaryfilm) Following the screening there will be a Q&A session with director Shahin Armin. Tickets are limited, so if you’re interested reserve them now.


Shahin Armin & Sohrab Daryabandari
